subtitulo: Joining ideas so the listener can follow
descripcion: At B2 the sentences are usually correct but they sit next to each other without a visible connection. Discourse markers are the words that show the reader how one idea relates to the next: adding, contrasting, giving a reason, drawing a conclusion. Learning ten and using them well is worth more than knowing fifty.

cuadroReferencia.notaPie: The left column is not "worse" English: it is the right register for speaking. Using the right column out loud sounds like reading an essay.

ejemplos.texto: *I started the course late. That said, I caught up within a month.*
*The classes were online, so I could study after work.*
*It's a long course. On top of that, it's expensive.*
*It was hard. I enjoyed it, though.*
*All in all, it was worth it.*

notas: *Though* at the end of a sentence is very common in speech: *It was hard. I enjoyed it, though.*
*So* and *because* answer opposite questions. *Because* gives the reason, *so* gives the result. Learners often swap them.
One marker per sentence is enough. Two in a row cancel each other out.

contraste.es: Spanish formal writing often builds long sentences with several linked clauses, while English prefers shorter sentences joined with markers (however, as a result). Translating a Spanish paragraph sentence by sentence can produce one very long English sentence.
contraste.de: German formal writing often packs several subordinate clauses into one sentence, while English prefers shorter sentences joined with markers. The German word also is a false friend: it means so, not also.
contraste.it: Italian formal writing often uses long, complex sentences, while English prefers shorter ones joined with markers (however, so). Quindi corresponds well to so.
contraste.fr: French formal writing often uses long sentences, while English prefers shorter ones joined with markers. Donc corresponds well to so, and cependant to however.
contraste.pt: Portuguese formal writing often uses long sentences, while English prefers shorter ones joined with markers. Portanto corresponds well to so, and no entanto to however.

errores: *In the other hand* — it is *on the other hand*.
*Also* at the start of a spoken sentence sounds abrupt; *and also* or *on top of that* is more natural.
*Although* and *but* together: *Although it was hard, but I finished.* Only one is needed.
*For example* followed by a whole clause with no example in it.

es: *en cambio* rendered as *in change* instead of *on the other hand* or *whereas*.
de: *zwar … aber* rendered with *indeed* in every concession: *It is indeed expensive, but good* instead of *It may be expensive, but it's good*.
it: *invece* rendered as *instead* for a contrast: *I like tea, instead he likes coffee* instead of *whereas he likes coffee*.
fr: *en revanche* rendered as *in revenge* instead of *on the other hand*.
pt: *em compensação* rendered as *in compensation* instead of *on the other hand*.

traducciones.pt: a aprendizagem ao longo da vida

mision.consigna: Explain a course or training you did, why you chose it and whether it was worth it.

microtareas.texto: Write four pairs of sentences with no marker. Then join each pair.
Take a paragraph you wrote and replace every *and* with a more precise marker.
Record 90 seconds about something you learned recently. Use *that said* once.

autochequeo: Eight different markers, or three repeated?
Any written-only marker in a spoken piece?
Did I use *although* and *but* in the same sentence?
Does every *for example* actually introduce an example?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on discourse markers and linking. (1) Mark each one and say if it fits the meaning and the register. (2) Show me two places where a marker was missing and the reader has to guess the connection. (3) Flag repeated markers. Do not correct anything else.
